scenes.note: FACE, full size. This is the hook. Smile before the first word. Say it to the lens, from memory if you can. One notch more energy than feels normal.
lines: Right. Take a zinc-copper cell. I lift the salt bridge out, and the current drops to zero. Straight away.
But the electrons don't even go through the salt bridge. They go through the wire. So what was that little tube actually doing? That's today's question.

scenes.t: Charge builds up: the zinc side
scenes.note: Voice and pen. Draw the + charges building up in the zinc half-cell as you talk. Slow and clear.
lines: Suppose the electrons could keep flowing with no bridge.
Look at the zinc half-cell first. Zinc atoms keep turning into zinc two plus ions. So positive charge builds up in that solution.

scenes.t: Charge builds up: the copper side
scenes.note: Voice and pen. Draw the − charges building up in the copper half-cell.
lines: Now the copper side. Copper two plus ions are being removed, because they're turning into copper. The negative ions in that solution get left behind. So negative charge builds up there.
Within a moment, that build-up would stop the flow. The bridge stops the build-up.

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the cell with the potassium nitrate bridge. Ask the question, then stay quiet for 3 seconds. The lesson stops there for the learner.
lines: Your turn to think. The salt bridge is potassium nitrate. Which ions move out of the bridge into the zinc half-cell? Pause the lesson and write it down.
The nitrate ions. They're negative, so they move into the zinc half-cell, where positive charge is building up.

scenes.note: Voice and pen. Draw the arrows for both kinds of ion.
lines: At the same time, potassium ions move into the copper half-cell, where copper two plus ions are being removed.
Ions from each half-cell move into the bridge too. So ions move both ways.

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the two functions, appearing as you say them. Exam voice: this is where the marks are.
lines: Now, how do you get the marks? The memo wants two functions. One: it completes the circuit. Two: it maintains electrical neutrality in the half-cells.
If you have to describe it, name the ions and name the half-cells. Just writing that ions flow through the salt bridge gets you nothing on its own.

scenes.note: FACE. This is the exam trap: say it to the lens, from memory. Lean in a little.
lines: Here's the one I see in every test. Electrons do not go through the salt bridge. Ever.
Electrons stay in the wire and the electrodes. In the solutions and in the bridge, it's ions that carry the charge.

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the lab's salt bridge choices. Steady pace.
lines: Last thing: which salt do we use? The ions in the bridge must not react with the ions in either half-cell.
That's why potassium nitrate is the usual choice. Nitrates don't form precipitates.

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the silver half-cell, then the permanganate half-cell. Steady pace.
lines: Potassium chloride won't work next to a silver half-cell. The chloride ions react with the silver ions to form a white precipitate of silver chloride. That removes silver ions from that half-cell.
Next to an acidified permanganate half-cell it fails for a different reason. Permanganate is a stronger oxidising agent than chlorine, so it oxidises the chloride ions.

scenes.note: Voice only. Warm finish: smile as you say it (people can hear a smile).
lines: Over to you. Next in the app is See it happen. Open the Build a cell lab, change the salt bridge, and watch what each choice does to the voltage. Then Train. Then Check. See you there.

roomTone.note: Dog out, door shut, phone silent, fan off. Sit still and say nothing for 10 seconds. I use this to take out the background hum.
